summary: In Capernaum a Gentile centurion asks Jesus to heal his dying servant with only a word, and Jesus marvels at his faith and heals the servant from a distance.
key_insight: Only twice do the Gospels say that Jesus marveled. Here a Gentile soldier amazed Him by his faith; in Nazareth His own townspeople amazed Him by their unbelief (Mark 6:6).
story: When Jesus had finished His sayings to the people, He entered Capernaum. {Lk} A centurion there had a servant who was dear to him, {Lk} lying at home paralyzed and dreadfully tormented, {Mt} sick and ready to die. {Lk}

Hearing about Jesus, the centurion sent elders of the Jews to plead with Him to come and heal his servant. They begged Him earnestly, saying the man deserved it, “for he loves our nation, and has built us a synagogue.” {Lk} Jesus said, “I will come and heal him,” {Mt} and He went with them. {Lk}

When Jesus was not far from the house, the centurion sent friends with a message: “Lord, do not trouble Yourself, for I am not worthy that You should enter under my roof.” He had not even thought himself worthy to come to Jesus. {Lk} “But only speak a word, and my servant will be healed. For I also am a man under authority, having soldiers under me. And I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes.” {Mt}

When Jesus heard it, He marveled. He turned to the crowd following Him {Lk} and said, “Assuredly, I say to you, I have not found such great faith, not even in Israel!” Many would come from east and west and sit down with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, while the sons of the kingdom would be cast out into outer darkness. {Mt}

Then Jesus said to the centurion, “Go your way; and as you have believed, so let it be done for you.” His servant was healed that same hour. {Mt} When the messengers returned to the house, they found the servant well. {Lk}
differences: In Matthew the centurion speaks to Jesus himself. In Luke he sends Jewish elders and then friends, and he never meets Jesus face to face.
Matthew says the servant was paralyzed and dreadfully tormented; Luke says he was sick and ready to die, and dear to his master.
Only Luke records the elders’ praise: the centurion loved the nation and built the synagogue.
Only Matthew records the saying about many coming from east and west while the sons of the kingdom are cast out. Luke has a similar saying later (Luke 13:28–29).
Matthew ends with Jesus’ word to the centurion and the healing “that same hour”; Luke ends with the messengers finding the servant well.

fit.question: Matthew says the centurion came to Jesus and spoke with Him. Luke says he sent elders and then friends, because he did not think himself worthy to come. Did he come or not?

points.label: Speaking through messengers
points.text: In the ancient world, what a man did through his agents was said to be done by him, much as we say a president signed a treaty his ambassador delivered. John’s Gospel shows the same habit: Jesus “made and baptized more disciples than John,” though His disciples did the baptizing (John 4:1–2).

points.label: Matthew shortens, Luke fills in
points.text: Matthew often tells a story briefly and goes straight to the main exchange. Here he keeps the centurion’s words and Jesus’ answer and leaves out the go-betweens. Luke gives the fuller sequence of who carried the message.

fit.note: Matthew reports the centurion’s words as his own because they were his own; Luke shows how they reached Jesus.
fit.short: The centurion spoke through elders and friends. Matthew credits the words to the man who sent them; Luke shows the messengers.

scene.label: A centurion
scene.text: A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers. In Galilee he probably served Herod Antipas, whose troops were organized on the Roman pattern. He was a Gentile, yet respected by the Jewish elders of the town.

scene.label: Under my roof
scene.text: Strict Jews avoided entering a Gentile’s house, which they counted unclean (Acts 10:28). The centurion may have known this and wished to spare Jesus the problem.

scene.label: The synagogue at Capernaum
scene.text: Visitors to Capernaum today see the ruins of a white limestone synagogue from the fourth or fifth century AD. It stands on a foundation of dark basalt that many archaeologists think belongs to an earlier synagogue, possibly the one this centurion built.

scene.label: The feast with Abraham
scene.text: The prophets pictured the age to come as a great feast for all peoples (Isaiah 25:6), and Jews expected to share it with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Jesus says Gentiles will sit at that table, while some who assumed a place will be shut out.

witnesses.matthew: Places this healing second in his chain of miracles after the sermon, right after Jesus touches a leper. A Gentile soldier shows greater faith than Israel, and only Matthew places here the warning that many from east and west will sit at the feast while the sons of the kingdom are cast out.
witnesses.luke: Gives the full sequence: the Jewish elders, the gifts to the nation, the friends sent with the message. Writing for Gentile readers like Theophilus, Luke shows a Gentile respected by Jews and humble before Jesus, a preview of Cornelius, another God-fearing centurion (Acts 10:1–2).

seeing.reveals: Jesus’ word has authority over sickness at a distance, and He marvels at faith wherever He finds it. He welcomes a Gentile to the table of Abraham on the strength of his trust.
seeing.living: The centurion knew he was unworthy and still asked boldly. Come to Jesus the same way, without pointing to what you have done for Him, and trust His word even when you cannot see Him act.
seeing.ponder: Do you take Jesus at His word when you cannot see Him act, or do you need Him to come under your roof first?

preaching.big_idea: The unworthy may trust Jesus’ word completely, and He calls that great faith.
outline: A need that crossed a divide (1–3)
A message of unworthiness and trust (6–8)
A faith that made Jesus marvel (9–10)
preaching.watch_for: The elders say the centurion is “deserving” (v. 4); his own message says, “I did not even think myself worthy to come to You” (v. 7). The two words share one Greek root. Jesus does not praise what the elders praised; He marvels at faith.
